etymology: From Old English besēcan, “to seek diligently, ask earnestly,” an intensive of sēcan (to seek). Renders the Greek parakaleō, “to call alongside, urge, entreat,” and deōmai, “to beg of need.”
biblical_def: Beseeching is earnest, pressing, often tearful entreaty—the urgent calling-alongside of one party by another, whether of man to God, of man to man, or of God Himself to His creatures. It is no casual request. The biblical beseecher leans his whole soul into the asking: Paul beseeches the Roman brethren by the mercies of God to present their bodies a living sacrifice; he beseeches the Lord thrice that the thorn depart; he beseeches the Corinthian church as though God did beseech you by us, praying men in Christ’s stead, ‘Be ye reconciled to God.’ The word carries the freight of need, the posture of dependence, and the dignity of office: the apostle beseeches because he must, the saint beseeches because he cannot otherwise be heard, and the God of heaven Himself stoops to beseech rebellious sinners through His ambassadors. To beseech is to confess that one is not in command of the outcome, that the matter sought is too great to demand and too precious to leave alone, and that the only access is the open ear and yielded heart of the one entreated. The thread of beseeching runs through the whole counsel of God: Abraham beseeching for Sodom, Moses beseeching for Israel, Hannah beseeching for a son, Christ in Gethsemane beseeching the cup might pass, and the church at every age beseeching her Lord, the Spirit, and one another. It is prayer with its sleeves rolled up.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines BESEECH as to entreat; to supplicate; to implore; to ask or pray with urgency.
webster_full: BESEECH, v.t. — To entreat; to supplicate; to implore; to ask or pray with urgency; followed by for before the thing sought, as I beseech you for the prisoner; or by the simple object, as I beseech thee, hear me.
BESEECHING, ppr. — Entreating; supplicating; imploring with earnestness.
scriptures: Romans 12:1
I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service.
2 Corinthians 5:20
Now then we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God did beseech you by us: we pray you in Christ’s stead, be ye reconciled to God.
2 Corinthians 12:8
For this thing I besought the Lord thrice, that it might depart from me.
Ephesians 4:1
I therefore, the prisoner of the Lord, beseech you that ye walk worthy of the vocation wherewith ye are called.
corruption_summary: Beseeching is corrupted by the casual prayer register of the present age—the breezy “just”-littered request that asks God for things as one might tap an app, without the urgency, dependence, or pressing of soul that biblical beseeching carries.
corruption_paragraphs: The age has trained the worshipper out of beseeching. Prayer language has been flattened into a casual, conversational, almost transactional register: just want to lift up, just thinking of, just praying for—the word just functioning as a verbal apology for daring to ask at all. The urgency is gone. The pressing is gone. The willingness to be heard reluctantly, to wait, to wrestle, to entreat as though the outcome mattered eternally, has been replaced by a relaxed and unimpassioned register that would not recognize itself in Paul on his knees for the thorn, in Hannah pouring out her soul at Shiloh, or in Christ’s strong crying and tears in Gethsemane.

Beseeching is also corrupted by the inverse error—the demand-prayer of name-it-and-claim-it teaching, which mistakes pressing entreaty for boasted certainty and treats God as a vending machine activated by the right formula. Both errors collapse the biblical posture: the saint who beseeches knows he does not command the answer, yet asks with the urgency of one for whom the matter is everything. Recover beseeching, and prayer recovers both its weight and its trembling boldness—the suppliant calling alongside, leaning the whole soul into the asking, confident only that the ear of the Father is open to the Son in whose name he comes.
roots_summary: Greek parakaleō (to call alongside, entreat) and deōmai (to beg of need); Hebrew chānan (to plead for grace) and chālāh (to entreat the face of).
roots_lines: Greek parakaleō (G3870) — to call alongside, entreat, urge, comfort; the verb behind Paraclete.
Greek deōmai (G1189) — to beg, beseech, of conscious need.
Hebrew chānan (H2603, hithpael) — to plead for grace, make supplication.
Hebrew chālāh (H2470, piel) — to entreat or soften the face of, as in entreat the face of the LORD.
usage: Beseeching is prayer with its sleeves rolled up—urgent entreaty that leans the whole soul into the asking.
Paul does not request that the Romans present their bodies; he beseeches them, by the mercies of God—weight, not tone, is the difference.
The casual ‘just praying for’ register of the age would not recognize itself in Hannah at Shiloh or Christ in Gethsemane.

etymology: From Old French chastier, from Latin castigare, “to make pure, correct, discipline,” from castus (pure) + agere (to drive). Renders the Greek paideuō, “to train as a child, discipline,” and the Hebrew yāsar, “to discipline, instruct, correct.”
biblical_def: To chasten is to discipline by corrective sorrow—to train a son by the loving hand of a father who will not let him grow up a fool. It is not punishment that destroys but discipline that perfects; not vengeance but training; not the wrath that condemns but the rod that recovers. Chastening is the Father’s answer to His children’s sin and folly: whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth. The argument of Hebrews 12 is decisive: chastening is the credential of sonship, not its negation. A son God does not chasten is no son at all. The mark of the Father’s love is precisely that He will not leave His children to their wandering; He hedges them with affliction, makes the bed of self-indulgence uncomfortable, suffers them to feel the wage of their folly, takes from them what they have idolized, lays sickness, loss, frustration, and the discipline of unanswered prayer upon them—always in measure, always with the end of yielding the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby. Chastening is grievous in the moment, not joyous; the saint is not asked to enjoy the rod, only to receive it from the Father’s hand and to bow under it. The whole of providence is the Father’s training of His children: hard providences are not signs of His abandonment but of His discipline; the apparent silence of God is often the schoolroom in which His sons learn the deepest lessons of grace; and the unbroken absence of any chastening at all would be the most alarming sign a soul could meet.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines CHASTEN as to correct by punishment; to punish; to inflict pain for the purpose of reclaiming an offender; to afflict by other means; to humble.
webster_full: CHASTEN, v.t. — 1. To correct by punishment; to inflict pain for the purpose of reclaiming an offender; as, to chasten a son with a rod. 2. To afflict by other means than stripes, as God afflicts His people for their sins; to humble; to purify from errors or faults.
CHASTENING, n. — Correction; punishment for the purpose of reclaiming.
scriptures: Hebrews 12:6
For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth.
Proverbs 3:11-12
My son, despise not the chastening of the Lord; neither be weary of his correction: For whom the Lord loveth he correcteth; even as a father the son in whom he delighteth.
Revelation 3:19
As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten: be zealous therefore, and repent.
1 Corinthians 11:32
But when we are judged, we are chastened of the Lord, that we should not be condemned with the world.
corruption_summary: Chastening is corrupted by the therapeutic age that has equated all discipline with abuse, that cannot distinguish a Father’s rod from a tyrant’s lash, and that interprets every hard providence as evidence of divine indifference rather than divine love.
corruption_paragraphs: The therapeutic age cannot hear the word chasten. Discipline of any kind is suspected of being abuse; the rod of the loving father is conflated with the lash of the tyrant; and the very idea that God deliberately wounds His children for their healing is felt to be a defamation of His love. So the doctrine of chastening is muted in the modern pulpit, hard providences are explained away as accidents, the corrective sorrow of God is rebranded as a problem to be solved by counseling alone, and Hebrews 12 is read as a chapter to be endured rather than treasured. The saint who has lost the doctrine of chastening loses also the comfort of it—for if affliction is not the Father’s hand, it is only random pain, and there is no consolation in random pain.

Chastening is also corrupted at the opposite extreme by the harshness that mistakes any affliction for a sign of God’s wrath, that reads every hardship as judicial punishment, and that strips chastening of its loving and paternal character. The biblical doctrine holds the cord at both ends. Chastening is real: God does in fact discipline His children, hedges them in with affliction, and trains them by sorrow. And chastening is fatherly: it is administered by the loving hand of the One who delights in the son He corrects, never to destroy, always to recover, always in measure, always with the end of yielding the peaceable fruit of righteousness. Recover the doctrine, and the saint can kiss the rod, knowing whose hand wields it.
roots_summary: Greek paideuō (to train as a child) and Hebrew yāsar (to discipline, instruct)—the loving Father’s corrective training of His sons.
roots_lines: Greek paideuō (G3811) — to train as a child, discipline, educate (from pais, child).
Hebrew yāsar (H3256) — to discipline, chastise, instruct, admonish.
Hebrew mūsār (H4148) — discipline, correction, instruction (the noun of yāsar).
Greek paideia (G3809) — the noun: chastening, discipline, training—as in Heb 12:11.
usage: Chastening is the Father’s training of His sons by corrective sorrow—not vengeance, but the rod that recovers.
Whom the Lord loves He chastens—the unchastened soul, by that fact alone, has reason to question its sonship.
The therapeutic age cannot distinguish a Father’s rod from a tyrant’s lash and so loses both the doctrine and its comfort.

etymology: From Old English heorcnian, an intensive of hīeran (to hear)—to listen attentively, give heed. Renders the Hebrew shāma, “to hear so as to obey,” the keynote verb of Israel’s confession (Shema Yisrael), and the Greek akouō, “to hear.”
biblical_def: To hearken is to hear with the will engaged—to listen with a view to obeying, not merely to register sound. Scripture treats the ear as a moral organ: God’s controversy with His people is not that they have not heard, but that they have not hearkened, have not bowed the will to what the ear received. Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God is one LORD is no abstract proposition; it is a summons to ordered obedience. The whole Old Testament can be read as God’s pleading with a people who hear and do not hearken: they have ears, but they hear not; since the day that your fathers came forth out of the land of Egypt unto this day I have even sent unto you all my servants the prophets, daily rising up early and sending them: Yet they hearkened not unto me. Hearkening is the inner motion that translates revelation into obedience. It is what Mary did when she said be it unto me according to thy word; it is what Samuel learned when he answered speak; for thy servant heareth; it is what the wise man does who, hearing his father’s instruction, performs it; and it is what the foolish man refuses. To hearken is therefore the first act of faith and the chief act of the disciple: the ear that hears and the heart that yields. The mark of the sheep, Christ said, is precisely this: my sheep hear my voice, and they follow me—hearing fused with following, hearkening as the inner shape of discipleship.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines HEARKEN as to listen; to lend the ear; to attend to what is uttered, with eagerness or curiosity; hence, in scripture, to hear with attention and obey.
webster_full: HEARKEN, v.i. — 1. To listen; to lend the ear; to attend to what is uttered, with eagerness or curiosity; as, to hearken to a story or a lecture. 2. In scripture, to attend with submission or obedience; to obey; as, to hearken to the voice of the Lord; the people would not hearken to the prophet.
HEARKENING, ppr. — Listening; attending to; obeying.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 6:4
Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD.
1 Samuel 15:22
Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams.
Jeremiah 7:25-26

Since the day that your fathers came forth out of the land of Egypt unto this day I have even sent unto you all my servants the prophets... Yet they hearkened not unto me, nor inclined their ear, but hardened their neck.
John 10:27
My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.
corruption_summary: Hearkening is corrupted by the listening culture that mistakes the registering of words for the bowing of the will—the podcast-and-sermon-consuming age that hears more, retains more, and obeys less than any generation that has come before it.
corruption_paragraphs: Never has more religious teaching reached the ear of the church, and never has the ear been less a moral organ. The believer of the present age has access to the world’s great preachers on demand, can consume sermons by the hour while driving, may sit under more careful exposition in a week than the medieval saint heard in a lifetime—and yet the practical obedience of the same believer is often visibly thinner than that of his unlettered forebears. The breakdown is at hearkening. The age has trained the ear to hear without bowing the will; sermons are taken as content to evaluate, not as the voice of God to obey; the very abundance of teaching cultivates the posture of the consumer, who samples and rates and moves on, rather than the posture of the disciple, who hears in order to do.

Scripture’s rebuke is sharp: be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves. The hearer-only is a man who looks at his face in a mirror and forthwith forgets what manner of man he was; the hearkener is the man who, having heard, goes and does. Recover the doctrine that the ear is a moral organ, that to hear is to be obligated, that God speaks not to inform but to command, and that the sheep of His pasture are known not by how much teaching they consume but by how readily they follow the Shepherd’s voice—and the consumer-listener is reformed back into the disciple-hearkener God means His sheep to be.
roots_summary: Hebrew shāma (to hear so as to obey)—the verb of the Shema—and Greek akouō (to hear, often with obedience implied), with hupakouō as the explicit hear-under, obey.
roots_lines: Hebrew shāma (H8085) — to hear, listen, obey; the keynote verb of the Shema in Deut 6:4.
Greek akouō (G191) — to hear, to listen, sometimes with implicit obedience.
Greek hupakouō (G5219) — to hear-under, to obey (the fused form makes the relation explicit).
Hebrew qāshab (H7181) — to incline the ear, attend carefully—the posture-of-the-ear word.
usage: Hearkening is hearing with the will engaged—the ear that bows the soul, not merely registers sound.
To obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams—Samuel’s rebuke is still the standard.
The age consumes more teaching than any before and hearkens to it less—the ear is a moral organ, and ours has been numbed.

etymology: From Latin mortificare, “to put to death,” from mors (death) + facere (to make). Renders the Greek nekroō, “to make dead, kill,” and thanatoō, “to put to death.”
biblical_def: To mortify is to put to death—specifically, to put to death the deeds of the body, the members which are upon the earth, the indwelling motions of sin which yet remain in the believer. It is the violent, deliberate, daily work of the regenerate soul against its own corruptions, in the strength of the Holy Spirit, on the ground of union with Christ. Paul’s twin texts are decisive: if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live, and mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth; fornication, uncleanness, inordinate affection, evil concupiscence, and covetousness, which is idolatry. The figure is not metaphor for management; it is execution. The remaining sin in the believer is not to be befriended, negotiated with, managed, or contained: it is to be killed. The Puritan John Owen’s axiom states the doctrine: be killing sin or it will be killing you. Mortification is not the work of an hour or a season but of the whole Christian life—the daily, painful, often bloody application of the cross of Christ to specific sins by the power of the Spirit. It is impossible apart from union with the crucified Christ, who broke the dominion of sin at the cross, and apart from the Spirit, by whom alone the deeds of the body are put to death. It is grievous to the flesh, because the flesh is what is being killed; it is necessary to life, because the alternative is being killed by what one refuses to kill. The doctrine of mortification rebukes both the antinomian who treats remaining sin as harmless and the moralist who tries to mortify in his own strength—and recalls the saint to the Spirit-empowered, cross-grounded, daily war on the corruptions of his own heart.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines MORTIFY as to destroy the vital functions of; to subdue or bring into subjection by abstinence or rigorous severities; in theology, to subdue inordinate passions and appetites.
webster_full: MORTIFY, v.t. — 1. To destroy the vital functions of; as, to mortify flesh or animal substances. 2. To subdue or bring into subjection by abstinence or rigorous severities; as, to mortify the flesh. 3. To humble; to depress; to abase, as pride; to affect with humiliating chagrin.
In theology: To subdue or destroy the activity of carnal appetites and inclinations; to bring the flesh and its lusts into subjection by self-denial and the help of divine grace.
scriptures: Romans 8:13
For if ye live after the flesh, ye shall die: but if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live.
Colossians 3:5
Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth; fornication, uncleanness, inordinate affection, evil concupiscence, and covetousness, which is idolatry.
Galatians 5:24
And they that are Christ’s have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts.
Romans 6:11
Likewise reckon ye also yourselves to be dead indeed unto sin, but alive unto God through Jesus Christ our Lord.
corruption_summary: Mortification is corrupted, on one side, by the antinomian grace-talk that treats remaining sin as harmless and recoils from the very language of killing; and on the other, by the moralism that tries to mortify in fleshly strength rather than by the Spirit and on the ground of union with Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Mortification is a doctrine the present church largely refuses to preach. The very word survives chiefly in the trivialized sense of I was mortified—reduced from the Spirit’s violent execution of indwelling sin to an emotion of social embarrassment. The substantive doctrine has been displaced by a soft grace-talk that treats remaining sin as either too tender to confront, too complex to address directly, or insufficiently serious to warrant violent language. The result is congregations who hear constantly that they are loved and accepted in Christ—both gloriously true—and who never hear that they are also commanded to put to death the indwelling motions of fornication, anger, covetousness, and pride that still war in their members. Antinomian grace without mortification breeds sleek, comfortable, slowly-dying souls who never learn that the gospel which justifies them also commands the daily killing of the sin from which they were justified.

The opposite corruption is moralism—the attempt to mortify in fleshly strength, by sheer willpower, by behavioral programs, by accountability software, by the discipline of the natural man. This too misses the doctrine. Biblical mortification is through the Spirit and on the ground of union with the crucified Christ: the flesh has been crucified with him, and the same Spirit who raised Christ from the dead now applies that crucifixion to the indwelling sin of the believer. Mortify in your own strength and you exchange one set of sins for another, often more religious and more dangerous. Mortify by the Spirit on the ground of the cross, and the deeds of the body are truly put to death and the soul truly lives. Owen’s great work on mortification is not optional reading for the serious saint; it is the manual of the regenerate man’s daily war against himself.
roots_summary: Greek nekroō (to make dead, kill—Col 3:5) and thanatoō (to put to death—Rom 8:13), both grounded in the believer’s union with the crucified Christ.
roots_lines: Greek nekroō (G3499) — to make dead, to deaden; the verb of Col 3:5, “mortify therefore your members.”
Greek thanatoō (G2289) — to put to death; the verb of Rom 8:13, “mortify the deeds of the body.”
Greek stauroō (G4717) — to crucify; in Gal 5:24, “they that are Christ’s have crucified the flesh.”
Latin mortificare — to make dead, the source of the English verb; the Vulgate’s rendering of the Greek death-verbs.
usage: Be killing sin or it will be killing you—Owen’s axiom states the whole doctrine in one line.
Mortification is not metaphor for management; it is execution—the daily, Spirit-empowered putting to death of indwelling corruption.
Antinomian grace without mortification breeds sleek, slowly-dying souls; moralism without the Spirit produces religious sins more dangerous than the ones replaced.

etymology: From Latin discernere, “to separate, distinguish,” from dis- (apart) + cernere (to sift, separate). Renders the Greek diakrinō, “to judge through, distinguish,” and the Hebrew bīn, “to perceive, understand, distinguish between.”
biblical_def: To discern is to distinguish—to sift the true from the false, the precious from the vile, the spirit of truth from the spirit of error, the wisdom from above from the wisdom that is earthly, sensual, devilish. Discernment is not opinion, intuition, or the modern ‘vibe’-reading by which the present age judges; it is the trained capacity of the spiritual man to apply the standards of Scripture to the matters before him and to render a sound judgment. Paul prays for the Philippians that their love may abound in knowledge and in all judgment; that ye may approve things that are excellent; the writer to the Hebrews rebukes immature believers who, though they ought to be teachers, still need the first principles, and explains that strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil. Discernment is therefore the fruit of exercise—the long, patient, Scripture-soaked use of the spiritual senses on real cases, by which the mature believer learns to distinguish what looks alike but is not the same. The Spirit grants a particular gift of discerning of spirits for the testing of prophets and teachers; every believer is commanded to try the spirits, whether they are of God, and to test all things, holding fast that which is good. Apart from discernment, the church is a sitting target for every wind of doctrine, every plausible heresy, every gospel-counterfeit dressed in evangelical language; with it, she is what Christ means her to be—a body able to recognize her Shepherd’s voice and to flee from strangers.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines DISCERN as to separate by the eye or by the understanding; to distinguish; to see the difference between; to make distinction; as, to discern between good and evil.
webster_full: DISCERN, v.t. — 1. Literally, to separate by the eye or by the understanding. Hence, to distinguish; to see the difference between; as, to discern the blossom-buds from the leaf-buds of plants. 2. To know or perceive the difference; to make distinction; as, to discern between good and evil, truth and falsehood. 3. To discover by the eye or the understanding; to perceive.
DISCERNING, ppr. or a. — Distinguishing; seeing the difference; knowing; judging.
scriptures: Hebrews 5:14
But strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil.
1 Corinthians 12:10
To another the working of miracles; to another prophecy; to another discerning of spirits...
1 John 4:1
Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world.
Philippians 1:9-10
And this I pray, that your love may abound yet more and more in knowledge and in all judgment; That ye may approve things that are excellent.
corruption_summary: Discernment is corrupted by the subjectivized ‘vibe’-reading of the present age that judges teachers and teachings by feel rather than by the standard of Scripture, and by the opposite error of harsh, untrained, online ‘discernment ministries’ that mistake suspicion for the Spirit’s gift.
corruption_paragraphs: The present age has replaced discernment with vibe-reading. The believer no longer asks of a teacher, does he handle the Word rightly? does he confess the historic faith? does his life match his doctrine?—but instead asks do I feel safe with him? does he resonate? does he affirm me? The standard is felt subjectivity rather than the objective rule of Scripture. The inevitable result is that teachers who feel warm are received though they teach error, and teachers who feel sharp are rejected though they teach truth; the church is sorted by affect rather than by doctrine, and discernment—the trained capacity to sift true from false by the standard of the Word—atrophies into nothing.

The opposite corruption is the suspicion-mongering of much of online ‘discernment’ culture, which mistakes the gift of the Spirit for the temperament of the perpetually offended, and which treats every doctrinal difference as occasion for an exposé. Real discernment is grave, charitable, slow to denounce, careful with charges, and grounded in long use of the spiritual senses on the Word; it is not the hair-trigger declaration that this or that brother is a heretic on the basis of a clip taken out of context. Recover both ends: discernment that is anchored in Scripture and not in vibes, and that is exercised with gravity and charity, not by reflex denunciation. The mature church is the discerning church—and the discerning church is the safe one.
roots_summary: Greek diakrinō (to judge through, distinguish) and Hebrew bīn (to perceive, understand, distinguish)—the trained sifting of true from false by the standard of the Word.
roots_lines: Greek diakrinō (G1252) — to judge through, distinguish, discriminate; the discerning of spirits in 1 Cor 12:10 is diakriseis pneumatōn.
Greek anakrinō (G350) — to examine, judge upward—in 1 Cor 2:14-15, the spiritual man judgeth all things.
Hebrew bīn (H995) — to perceive, understand, discern, distinguish.
Hebrew yāda (H3045) — to know experientially—the substrate of biblical discernment.
usage: Discernment is the trained capacity to sift the true from the false by the standard of Scripture—not opinion, intuition, or vibe.
Strong meat belongs to those whose senses are exercised by use to discern good and evil—discernment is the fruit of exercise.
Vibe-reading is not the gift of the Spirit, and suspicion-mongering is not its substitute—biblical discernment is grave, charitable, and Word-anchored.

etymology: From Old French entraitier, “to treat, handle,” from Latin tractare (to handle, deal with). Renders several biblical verbs: the Hebrew chālāh, “to soften the face of,” the Hebrew ‘āthar, “to entreat, pray,” and the Greek parakaleō, “to call alongside, beseech.”
biblical_def: To entreat is to plead with another, to beg favor, to soften the face of the one entreated, to seek by pressing request what cannot be demanded. It is the verb of supplication and the verb of personal pleading—Moses entreats the LORD to take away the plague, the Philistines entreat Samuel that he not cease to cry unto God for them, Isaac entreats the LORD for his barren wife Rebekah and the LORD is entreated of him. The Hebrew picture in chālāh is striking: to entreat the face of the LORD is to come near enough to ask Him to look upon one with favor, to soften His countenance, to be moved. The Greek parakaleō carries the picture of one called alongside—a near, personal pleading, not the formal address of a stranger. Entreaty therefore belongs to a relationship: one entreats a father, a friend, a covenant Lord; one does not entreat a stranger or a tyrant, only petitions or appeases them. Paul entreats Philemon for Onesimus rather than commanding; he charges Timothy not to rebuke an elder, but to entreat him as a father; James commends the wisdom from above as easy to be intreated—reasonable, approachable, open to pleading. Entreaty in Scripture therefore has two faces: the suppliant’s pleading, and the entreated’s yielded, approachable spirit. To be easy to be intreated is a mark of heavenly wisdom; to be hard to be intreated—closed, rigid, unmoved—is the temper of fallen pride.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ENTREAT as to ask earnestly; to beseech; to petition or pray with urgency; to supplicate; to solicit pressingly.
webster_full: ENTREAT, v.t. — 1. To ask earnestly; to beseech; to petition or pray with urgency; to supplicate; to solicit pressingly; as, I entreat you to forgive the offence. 2. To treat, in the obsolete sense of dealing with; as, they entreated him shamefully (Mark 12:4).
ENTREATY, n. — Urgent prayer; earnest petition; pressing solicitation.
scriptures: Genesis 25:21
And Isaac intreated the LORD for his wife, because she was barren: and the LORD was intreated of him, and Rebekah his wife conceived.
1 Timothy 5:1
Rebuke not an elder, but intreat him as a father; and the younger men as brethren.
James 3:17
But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, and easy to be intreated, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy.
2 Corinthians 8:4
Praying us with much intreaty that we would receive the gift, and take upon us the fellowship of the ministering to the saints.
corruption_summary: Entreaty is corrupted by the assertive, demand-shaped speech of the age, in which one does not plead with a brother or a Father but issues claims—and by the inverse, the hardened pride that is not easy to be entreated, that closes its face against the pleading of others.
corruption_paragraphs: The age has lost the register of entreaty. In a culture trained to assert rather than ask, to claim rights rather than to plead favor, the very posture of entreating—the suppliant face, the patient request, the willingness to wait, the readiness to be refused—feels weak and out of date. The believer absorbs this register and brings it before God: he no longer entreats the LORD; he announces his needs as one entitled to a response, declares his prayers in the assertive voice of the rights-bearing citizen, and is offended when answer is delayed. Recover the biblical word, and the saint recovers also the biblical posture: Isaac entreating for his barren wife, Moses entreating for rebellious Israel, the church entreating her Lord for the salvation of her city—pleading, not claiming; suppliant, not assertive; near, not commanding.

Entreaty is also corrupted at the receiving end—in the proud, closed, hard-to-be-entreated spirit that James contrasts with the wisdom from above. The man whose face cannot be softened, who cannot be reasoned with, whose decisions are not open to the pleading of a friend or a wife or a brother, has the temper of fallen pride dressed in the language of conviction. The wisdom from above is precisely easy to be intreated: open, reasonable, willing to be moved by good cause, slow to hold the line on personal preference and quick to yield where it can. The husband, the father, the elder, the boss, the pastor whose face is closed is unlike the heavenly Father, who is entreated of His people—and unlike the Christ who is touched with the feeling of our infirmities. Recover the doctrine: plead with God; be open to the pleading of others; and you will look more like the Father whose face His children may yet entreat.
roots_summary: Hebrew chālāh (to soften the face of) and ‘āthar (to entreat, pray); Greek parakaleō (to call alongside, beseech) and the related eupeithēs (easy to be entreated—James 3:17).
roots_lines: Hebrew chālāh (H2470, piel) — to entreat or soften the face of (the LORD).
Hebrew ‘āthar (H6279) — to entreat, supplicate, pray; used of Isaac’s prayer for Rebekah in Gen 25:21.
Greek parakaleō (G3870) — to call alongside, beseech, entreat.
Greek eupeithēs (G2138) — easy to be entreated, compliant, persuadable; the heavenly-wisdom adjective of James 3:17.
usage: Entreaty is the verb of relationship—one entreats a father, a friend, a covenant Lord; strangers and tyrants are merely petitioned.
The wisdom from above is easy to be intreated—reasonable, approachable, open to pleading; the temper of pride is the closed face.
The assertive, demand-shaped speech of the age has unlearned entreaty—and prayer suffers for it.

etymology: From Old English forgiefan, “to give utterly, give up,” from for- (intensive) + giefan (give). Renders the Greek aphiēmi, “to let go, send away,” and charizomai, “to give graciously”; and the Hebrew sālach, “to forgive,” and nāsā, “to lift, bear away.”
biblical_def: To forgive is to remit a debt that is truly owed—to release the offender from the just demand of the offence, not by pretending it did not happen, not by minimizing its weight, but by absorbing its cost in oneself and refusing to exact it from the one who owed it. The biblical word-pictures are vivid: aphiēmi sends the sin away, dismisses it, lets it go; charizomai gives graciously, treating the offence as the occasion of a free gift; the Hebrew nāsā lifts and bears the sin so that it no longer presses upon the offender; sālach is the verb God uses of His own pardon of His people. All these turn on the same reality: a real debt, a real cost, a real release. Forgiveness is therefore costly, not cheap; it is grace, not mere niceness. The cross stands at the center of the Christian doctrine of forgiveness, because there alone God forgives sin without compromise of justice: the debt is fully paid in the substitutionary suffering of His Son, so that He may be just and the justifier of him that believeth in Jesus. From that fountain the believer is to forgive: forgiving one another, even as God for Christ’s sake hath forgiven you. The horizontal forgiveness commanded of the saint is patterned on the vertical forgiveness received—costly, free, full, and unaccompanied by the secret bookkeeping of resentment. Christ’s warning is grave: if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses. Not that forgiveness earns forgiveness, but that the heart which has been truly forgiven cannot remain unforgiving; the parable of the unmerciful servant has only one ending. Forgiveness in Scripture is therefore neither cheap (it costs the cross) nor optional (it is the very air of the kingdom)—and the church which forgives as her Lord forgives is the truest credential the gospel ever sets before the watching world.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines FORGIVE as to pardon; to remit, as an offence or debt; to overlook an offence, and treat the offender as not guilty.
webster_full: FORGIVE, v.t. — 1. To pardon; to remit, as an offence or debt; to overlook an offence, and treat the offender as not guilty. 2. To remit; as, to forgive a debt. The original sense is to give back; hence to give up the demand against an offender.
FORGIVENESS, n. — The act of forgiving; the pardon of an offender; remission of an offence, debt, or penalty; disposition to pardon; willingness to forgive.
scriptures: Ephesians 4:32
And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ’s sake hath forgiven you.
Matthew 6:14-15
For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you: But if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.
Colossians 3:13
Forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any: even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye.
Psalm 32:1
Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered.
corruption_summary: Forgiveness is corrupted, on one side, by the therapeutic version that detaches it from repentance and from the cross and reduces it to a self-help technique for the forgiver’s emotional wellbeing; and on the other, by the bitter refusal to forgive that hoards offences and forgets the parable of the unmerciful servant.
corruption_paragraphs: Therapeutic culture has rewritten forgiveness as a unilateral, self-directed exercise: forgive for your own sake, so that you can move on, so that the offender no longer occupies space in your head; forgiveness as emotional hygiene rather than as the release of a real debt; forgiveness divorced from any reckoning of justice, any call to repentance, any reference to the cross at which alone the unfathomable debt of human sin was actually paid. The result is a thinned, self-referential forgiveness that costs the forgiver nothing in particular and bears no resemblance to the costly, Christ-patterned, debt-absorbing release the New Testament commands. Recover the cross at the center, and forgiveness recovers its substance: a real debt, a real cost, a real release, given because we ourselves have been given vastly more.

The opposite corruption is the refusal to forgive that hoards offences in the heart, replays them at length, withholds reconciliation when reconciliation is offered, and lives in the slow poison of unforgiveness. Scripture is severe with this temper. The parable of the unmerciful servant says without softening that the forgiven slave who would not forgive his fellow was delivered to the tormentors; so likewise shall my heavenly Father do also unto you, if ye from your hearts forgive not every one his brother their trespasses. The unforgiving heart is incompatible with the kingdom of the forgiven. Where there is true repentance from the offender, forgiveness is to be extended fully; where there is not, the saint is still to lay down resentment, to commit the cause to God who judges righteously, to bless and not curse, to do good to them that hate, and to leave room for the wrath that is His and not ours. Between cheap forgiveness and bitter unforgiveness lies the costly, cross-shaped forgiveness of the Christian: full, free, debt-absorbing, patterned on the Father’s own pardon of His enemies through the blood of His Son.
roots_summary: Greek aphiēmi (to let go, send away) and charizomai (to give graciously); Hebrew sālach (forgive, used only of God) and nāsā (to lift, bear away).
roots_lines: Greek aphiēmi (G863) — to send away, let go, release, remit; the main NT verb for forgiveness.
Greek charizomai (G5483) — to give freely, to forgive graciously—forgiveness as the giving of a gift.
Hebrew sālach (H5545) — to pardon, forgive—used in the OT only of God’s pardon.
Hebrew nāsā (H5375) — to lift, bear away (sin)—the verb behind the imagery of removing transgression.
usage: Forgiveness is the release of a real debt at real cost—not pretending the offence did not occur, but absorbing it as God absorbed ours at the cross.
Therapeutic forgiveness self-references; biblical forgiveness cross-references—even as God for Christ’s sake hath forgiven you.
The unforgiving heart is incompatible with the kingdom of the forgiven—the parable of the unmerciful servant has only one ending.

etymology: From Latin praevalere, “to be stronger,” from prae- (before) + valere (to be strong, have force). Renders the Hebrew yākhol, “to be able, to overcome,” and gābar, “to be strong, prevail”; and the Greek ischuō and katischuō, “to be strong, to prevail against.”
biblical_def: To prevail is to be stronger than—to overcome, to gain the victory, to come off conqueror in a real contest. Scripture uses the word for both holy prevailings and unholy ones: Jacob wrestles with the Angel of the LORD and is told thou hast power with God and with men, and hast prevailed; the gates of hell shall not prevail against the church Christ is building; the Lion of the tribe of Judah hath prevailed to open the book and the seven seals; conversely, the river of Genesis 7 prevailed exceedingly upon the earth, and the Philistines prevailed against Israel when she sinned. Prevailing in the believer’s life is always a wrought thing, never a natural one; the saint prevails in prayer because God grants the wrestling, not because the suppliant is strong; the church prevails in her witness because Christ is with her, not because her strategies are clever; the martyr prevails over death because the Lamb has overcome before him and grants him the same victory in His name. The deepest theology of prevailing is christological: Christ Himself is the great Prevailer, the One who has overcome the world, who has triumphed openly over principalities and powers in His cross, who in the Apocalypse is heralded precisely as he that overcometh—and into whose victory all who are His are taken up. The saint’s prevailing is the application of Christ’s prevailing to his particular battles; the church’s prevailing is the historical outworking of Christ’s prevailing through the long centuries; the eschatological prevailing is the final unveiling of what has been true since the cross—the Lamb has overcome, and they that are with Him are called, and chosen, and faithful.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PREVAIL as to overcome; to gain the victory or superiority; to gain the advantage; to have the upper hand.
webster_full: PREVAIL, v.i. — 1. To overcome; to gain the victory or superiority; to gain the advantage; to have the upper hand. The Philistines prevailed against Israel. 2. To be in force; to have effect, power, or influence; to be predominant; as, the customs that prevail in a country. 3. To gain over by entreaty or persuasion; followed by upon; as, I prevailed upon him to relinquish his design.
PREVAILING, ppr. or a. — Overcoming; gaining the advantage; predominant; most general; efficacious.
scriptures: Genesis 32:28
And he said, Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel: for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed.
Matthew 16:18
And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.
Revelation 5:5
Weep not: behold, the Lion of the tribe of Juda, the Root of David, hath prevailed to open the book, and to loose the seven seals thereof.
1 John 5:4
For whatsoever is born of God overcometh the world: and this is the victory that overcometh the world, even our faith.
corruption_summary: Prevailing is corrupted by the self-empowerment register of the age, in which ‘you got this’ and ‘manifest your victory’ replace the Spirit-wrought, Christ-grounded prevailing the Bible knows—and by the inverse defeatism that forgets Christ has already overcome and walks as if the field were lost.
corruption_paragraphs: Therapeutic and self-empowerment culture has captured the language of prevailing and emptied it. Where Scripture speaks of the saint prevailing in prayer through wrestling with God, the modern motivational register speaks of the individual prevailing through belief in himself, manifestation, positive thinking, or grit. The agent has been swapped: the biblical Prevailer is the Lamb who has overcome and the Spirit who applies His victory to His saints; the modern prevailer is the self, leveraging mental technique. The vocabulary is sometimes Christian, but the theology is paganized: you got this replaces be strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might; manifest your victory replaces this is the victory that overcometh the world, even our faith. Recover Christ as the Prevailer, and the believer regains his true strength—the strength of the One into whose victory he has been taken up.

The opposite corruption is the practical defeatism that walks as if the church were a losing side, as if the gates of hell were in fact prevailing, as if Christ had not already triumphed openly over principalities and powers in His cross. Some of this defeatism wears the dress of theological seriousness—a sober pessimism about culture, the church, the age—but it can drift into denial of the actual victory of the Lamb, who has overcome and whose church He is building such that hell’s gates do not prevail. Recover both ends: the realism that knows the battle is hard and the eschatology that knows the outcome is settled. The saint and the church prevail because Christ has prevailed—and that is the only ground on which prevailing is ever spoken of in the Bible at all.
roots_summary: Hebrew yākhol (to be able, overcome) and gābar (to be strong, prevail); Greek ischuō and katischuō (to be strong, prevail against)—always with the great Prevailer, the Lamb, behind every saintly prevailing.
roots_lines: Hebrew yākhol (H3201) — to be able, to prevail, to overcome; used of Jacob’s prevailing in Gen 32.
Hebrew gābar (H1396) — to be strong, to prevail; root of gibbor, mighty man.
Greek ischuō (G2480) — to be strong, to have power, to prevail.
Greek katischuō (G2729) — to be strong against, to prevail over—the verb of Matt 16:18, “the gates of hell shall not prevail.”
usage: Prevailing in the believer’s life is always a wrought thing—the saint prevails because Christ has prevailed.
The gates of hell shall not prevail against the church Christ is building—practical defeatism is a quiet denial of His settled victory.
The self-empowerment register swaps the agent: you got this replaces be strong in the Lord, and the vocabulary survives while the theology has been paganized.

etymology: Verb form of prophecy; from Greek prophēteuō, “to speak forth from God,” from pro- (forth) + phēmi (to speak). Renders the Hebrew nābā’, “to prophesy, speak by divine inspiration.” Note the spelling: prophecy (n.); prophesy (v.).
biblical_def: To prophesy is to speak forth from God—to deliver the divine word as one commissioned by God to His people. The biblical prophet is not primarily a predictor of the future, though prediction is part of the office; he is first a herald of the LORD’s present message, an ambassador commissioned to declare thus saith the LORD to a covenant people, calling them back to the covenant, exposing their sin, comforting their afflictions, and announcing what God will yet do. Prophesying is therefore both forthtelling (declaring God’s word for the present hour) and foretelling (announcing God’s purposes for the future); the modern false dichotomy that pits these against each other misreads the office. The prophets of the Old Testament prophesied the coming of Christ, His sufferings, and the glory that should follow; the New Testament prophets speak by the Spirit to the churches; and Joel’s great promise—your sons and your daughters shall prophesy—is by Peter declared fulfilled at Pentecost, when the Spirit was poured out on all flesh. Paul ranks prophesying among the chief gifts the church is to covet: he that prophesieth speaketh unto men to edification, and exhortation, and comfort; and the Spirit’s gift of prophecy is to be exercised in the church according to the proportion of faith, judged by the others, and held under the rule of the apostolic Word. After the close of the canon, the prophetic office in its foundational, revelation-giving sense ceased; but the Spirit’s ongoing application of the prophetic Word, the preacher’s heralding of thus saith the LORD from the inspired text, and the saint’s Spirit-quickened speech to the brethren in edification, exhortation, and comfort all stand in the prophetic line. To prophesy in the church today is faithfully to declare God’s Word to God’s people in the power of the Spirit—and the office of preacher, far from being lesser than the apostolic prophet, is in this sense the prophetic office’s ordinary continuation.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PROPHESY as to foretell future events; to predict by divine inspiration; to utter predictions; also, to instruct in religious doctrines; to preach.
webster_full: PROPHESY, v.t. — 1. To foretell future events; to predict by divine inspiration. Of these also Enoch...prophesied. 2. To utter predictions; to foretell things to come. 3. To instruct in religious doctrines; to preach (1 Cor 14:3).
PROPHESYING, n. — The act or exercise of prediction or of preaching.
scriptures: Joel 2:28
And it shall come to pass afterward, that I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy...
1 Corinthians 14:3
But he that prophesieth speaketh unto men to edification, and exhortation, and comfort.
2 Peter 1:21
For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost.
Revelation 10:11
And he said unto me, Thou must prophesy again before many peoples, and nations, and tongues, and kings.
corruption_summary: Prophesying is corrupted, on one side, by the charismatic spectacle that turns it into stage-managed prediction and personal-word performance untethered from Scripture; and on the other, by the liberal critical tradition that strips the prophetic from any predictive or supernatural element and reduces the prophets to ethical social critics.
corruption_paragraphs: Large segments of the charismatic and self-styled prophetic movement have corrupted the office by turning it into spectacle. Prophets are platformed who issue dated predictions that routinely fail, who deliver personal words with no testable content, who blur the line between Scripture and their own impressions, and who escape accountability when their words do not come to pass by retrofitting them as conditional or symbolic. The biblical standard is the opposite: the prophet whose word does not come to pass was not sent of the LORD; the prophet who calls Israel after other gods is to be rejected though his sign does come to pass; and even the genuine New Testament gift is to be exercised in submission to the apostolic Word and judged by the church. Recover the standard, and the office is restored to its sober dignity: God’s Word delivered, with accountability, to God’s people.

The opposite corruption is the liberal critical reduction of the prophets to mere ethical critics—social commentators in religious dress, stripped of the predictive and supernatural element that the texts themselves insist upon. On this reading, the prophet does not actually foretell the coming of Christ, the destruction of Jerusalem, the return from exile, or the day of the LORD; he merely speaks moral truth to power in his own time. The doctrine of God’s sovereign foreknowledge collapses, and so does the apologetic weight of fulfilled prophecy, which Scripture itself sets forth as evidence of the LORD’s deity over against the idols. Recover both ends—sober, accountable forthtelling and the genuinely predictive prophetic element—and the office returns to its biblical shape: God’s herald, with God’s message, delivered with God’s authority, and vindicated by God’s providence.
roots_summary: Greek prophēteuō (to speak forth from God) and Hebrew nābā (to prophesy by divine inspiration)—forthtelling and foretelling alike under the rule of God’s Word.
roots_lines: Greek prophēteuō (G4395) — to speak forth from God, prophesy.
Greek prophētēs (G4396) — a prophet, one who speaks forth God’s message.
Hebrew nābā (H5012) — to prophesy, speak by divine inspiration.
Hebrew nābī (H5030) — a prophet, spokesman for God.
usage: To prophesy is to speak forth from God—both forthtelling His present word and foretelling His coming purposes.
Charismatic platforming of failed predictions and liberal reduction of the prophets to social critics both miss the office Scripture actually sets forth.
Faithful preaching of the inspired Word is the prophetic office’s ordinary continuation—the preacher stands in the prophetic line.

etymology: From Latin purgare, “to cleanse, purify,” from purus (pure) + agere (to drive). Renders the Greek katharizō, “to cleanse,” and the Hebrew kāphar, “to cover, atone,” and tāhēr, “to be clean.”
biblical_def: To purge is to cleanse by the removal of what defiles—to drive out the impurity that pollutes, leaving the thing or person pure. In Scripture the verb covers both ceremonial and moral cleansing, and its highest reference is to the purging of sin from the conscience by the blood of Christ. David prays, Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean—the Old Testament rite of cleansing pleaded as a figure of the deeper cleansing he longs for. The writer to the Hebrews sets the doctrine at its New-Covenant height: How much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without spot to God, purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God?—and again, when he had by himself purged our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high. The cross is the great purging: by it the Lord Jesus has accomplished the cleansing of His people once for all, putting away the sin which the blood of bulls and goats could only cover symbolically, and granting them a purged conscience to serve God in newness of life. Beyond that decisive purging, the saint is to be progressively purged in his sanctification: let us cleanse ourselves from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God; the vine is purged by the Husbandman (pruned) that it may bring forth more fruit; the precious metal is refined by the fire that the dross may be removed. Purging is therefore both definitive (accomplished at the cross and applied at conversion) and ongoing (the daily work of sanctification by Word and providence)—and both senses culminate in the final purging of the whole creation, when the elements shall melt with fervent heat and a new heavens and new earth shall emerge in which dwelleth righteousness.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PURGE as to cleanse or purify by separating and carrying off whatever is impure, heterogeneous, foreign, or superfluous; to clear from guilt or the imputation of guilt; in theology, to cleanse from the defilement of sin.
webster_full: PURGE, v.t. — 1. To cleanse or purify by separating and carrying off whatever is impure, heterogeneous, foreign, or superfluous; as, to purge a liquor; to purge the body; to purge the air. 2. To clear from guilt or the imputation of guilt; as, to purge oneself from the charge of treason. 3. In theology, to cleanse from the defilement of sin; to purify from moral pollution.
PURGING, n. — The act of cleansing or purifying; the carrying off of impure or noxious matter.
scriptures: Psalm 51:7
Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean: wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow.
Hebrews 1:3
Who being the brightness of his glory... when he had by himself purged our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high.
Hebrews 9:14
How much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without spot to God, purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God?
Malachi 3:3
And he shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver: and he shall purify the sons of Levi, and purge them as gold and silver.
corruption_summary: Purging is corrupted in the present age by its reduction to dieting fads (the ‘cleanse’ or ‘detox purge’) and to the cultural-political register of mass dismissal—both of which empty the word of its central biblical reference, the cleansing of the conscience and the soul from the defilement of sin by the blood of Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The word purge survives in the modern vocabulary chiefly in two flattened registers. The first is dietary: the juice cleanse, the detox purge, the wellness ritual that drives the impurities out of the body and leaves the spiritually unrenewed soul untouched. The second is political-cultural: the purge of an institution’s membership, the cancellation, the ideological cleansing of those judged impure on contemporary lines. Both have their place, real or contested; neither captures the substantive biblical doctrine, in which to purge is centrally to cleanse the conscience from the defilement of sin by the blood of Christ. The wellness register treats impurity as biochemical and addresses it with kale; the political register treats impurity as ideological and addresses it with expulsion; only the gospel treats impurity as the moral pollution of a fallen heart and addresses it with the blood of the Son of God.

Recover the biblical center and the secondary uses fall into proportion. The body is to be cared for, but the cleansing the soul needs is not dietary; the church and the institution must sometimes remove the impenitent, but the cleansing the conscience needs is not procedural. The doctrine of purging is at its core the doctrine of the cross: that Christ by Himself purged our sins, that His blood cleanses from all unrighteousness, that the conscience defiled by dead works is purged by the eternal-Spirit-offered sacrifice of the Son to serve the living God. With that purging accomplished, the saint walks in the ongoing sanctifying purgation of the vine pruned by the Husbandman and the silver refined by the fire—and toward the final purgation of a creation made new.
roots_summary: Greek katharizō (to cleanse) and Hebrew kāphar (to cover, atone)—the cleansing accomplished decisively by the blood of Christ in Hebrews 1:3 and 9:14.
roots_lines: Greek katharismos (G2512) — cleansing, purification (the noun behind catharsis).
Greek katharismon poiēsas — “having made purgation”—the participle of Heb 1:3 that summarizes the cross.
Hebrew kāphar (H3722) — to cover, atone—the Day-of-Atonement verb behind the purging of the holy place.
Hebrew tāhēr (H2891) — to be clean, to cleanse—the ceremonial purity verb.
usage: The cross is the great purging: when he had by himself purged our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high.
Purging is both definitive (at the cross, applied at conversion) and ongoing (the daily sanctifying pruning of the Vine’s Husbandman).
Wellness culture purges the body and politics purges the institution; only the gospel purges the conscience from dead works.

etymology: From Latin purificare, “to make pure,” from purus (pure) + facere (to make). Renders the Greek hagnizō, “to make holy, set apart for purity,” and the Hebrew tāhēr, “to be clean,” and zāqaq, “to refine, as metal.”
biblical_def: To purify is to make pure—to free a person or thing from defilement, so that it stands clean and fit for God. The biblical doctrine ranges across ceremonial purification (the rites of cleansing under the law), the moral purification of the heart by faith (Acts 15:9: purifying their hearts by faith), the practical purification of the believer’s life by the indwelling Spirit and the obeyed Word (1 Pet 1:22: ye have purified your souls in obeying the truth through the Spirit unto unfeigned love of the brethren), and the eschatological self-purification of the saint who hopes to see his Lord: every man that hath this hope in him purifieth himself, even as he is pure (1 John 3:3). The verb is therefore both passive and active: the believer is purified by Christ’s blood and by the Spirit (Tit 2:14: Christ gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify unto himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works); and the believer purifies himself in the daily mortification of sin and pursuit of holiness, in the strength of grace, with the hope of glory as motive. Purification is the great theme of the whole sanctifying enterprise: as the refiner sits over the silver, watching the dross come off until he can see his own face in the molten metal, so the Lord sits over His people, applying the fire of His Word, providence, and Spirit until the image of His Son is formed in them. The eschatological purification is the climax: at His coming, when we see Him as He is, we shall be like Him—the long work of purification carried to its completion in the resurrection body and the glorified soul.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PURIFY as to make pure or clear; to free from extraneous admixture; in a moral sense, to make pure; to free from guilt or the defilement of sin; in religion, to free from ceremonial uncleanness.
webster_full: PURIFY, v.t. — 1. To make pure or clear; to free from extraneous admixture; as, to purify liquors or metals. 2. To free from anything noxious or contagious; as, to purify the air. 3. In a moral sense, to make pure; to free from guilt or the defilement of sin; to free from improper mixture of any kind; as, to purify the heart. 4. In religion, to free from ceremonial uncleanness.
PURIFICATION, n. — The act of cleansing or making pure; in religion, a cleansing from the guilt of sin; also, the act of separating from anything noxious.
scriptures: 1 John 3:3
And every man that hath this hope in him purifieth himself, even as he is pure.
Titus 2:14
Who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify unto himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works.
Acts 15:9
And put no difference between us and them, purifying their hearts by faith.
Malachi 3:3
And he shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver: and he shall purify the sons of Levi, and purge them as gold and silver, that they may offer unto the LORD an offering in righteousness.
corruption_summary: Purification is corrupted by the aesthetic-and-wellness register of the age, which reduces purity to skincare regimens, ‘clean’ eating, and lifestyle hygiene, while the substantive doctrine of the heart purified by faith and the soul purified by the indwelling Spirit is forgotten.
corruption_paragraphs: The age has shifted purification from the moral to the aesthetic register. Where Scripture speaks of the heart purified by faith, the soul purified in obeying the truth, and the saint who in hope of his Lord’s appearing purifies himself even as He is pure, the contemporary culture speaks of skincare purification, ‘clean’ eating, detox routines, and lifestyle hygiene. The vocabulary survives; the referent has shifted. Purity has become a category of personal aesthetic and dietary cleanliness with no inward reference, while the inward purification on which Scripture insists—the cleansing of the heart, the conscience, and the affections by the blood and Spirit of Christ—is left largely unaddressed. The result is a generation that pursues aesthetic purity with religious intensity and inward purity with cultural indifference.

Recover the biblical center, and aesthetic purity falls into its modest place while moral purity returns to its proper urgency. The body is to be cared for; cleanliness is a small good. But the heart is what God watches, and the heart can be skincare-perfect and morally filthy at once. The doctrine of purification calls the saint to the daily, Spirit-empowered work of mortifying impurity in thought, affection, speech, and behavior; to the active hope of seeing Christ, which is the great motive of self-purification in 1 John 3; and to the patient endurance of the Refiner’s fire, by which the dross of indwelling sin is gradually removed until the image of the Son can be seen in the saint as in the refiner’s silver.
roots_summary: Greek hagnizō (to make holy, purify); Hebrew tāhēr (to be clean) and zāqaq (to refine, as metal)—the heart purified by faith, the soul purified by the Spirit, the saint purifying himself in hope of his Lord.
roots_lines: Greek hagnizō (G48) — to make pure, purify; the verb of 1 John 3:3 and Acts 21:24.
Greek hagnos (G53) — pure, chaste, holy (the adjective).
Hebrew tāhēr (H2891) — to be clean, pure—the major ceremonial-purity verb.
Hebrew zāqaq (H2212) — to refine, distill, purify (as gold or silver).
usage: Every man that has this hope in him purifies himself, even as He is pure—the saint’s active self-purification is hope-driven.
The heart is purified by faith and the soul by the Spirit; aesthetic cleanliness reaches neither.
Christ purified to Himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works—purification is part of redemption, not a separate program.

etymology: From Latin submittere, “to place under, lower,” from sub- (under) + mittere (to send, place). Renders the Greek hupotassō, a military term meaning “to arrange under, place in order under,” and the Hebrew kāna, “to humble, be subdued.”
biblical_def: To submit is to place oneself in the appointed order under God’s appointed authority—a glad, willing, principled arranging-of-self-under, not a forced subjugation. The Greek hupotassō is a military picture: troops arranged in rank under their commander, each man in his place, the order itself being the means of the army’s strength. Scripture commands a network of such ordered submissions: of all souls to God (submit yourselves therefore to God, Jas 4:7); of the church to Christ; of citizens to civil authorities (Rom 13:1); of believers one to another in the fear of God (Eph 5:21); of wives to their own husbands (Eph 5:22; 1 Pet 3:1); of children to parents (Eph 6:1); of younger to elder in the church (1 Pet 5:5); and of the flock to faithful elders (Heb 13:17). The pattern is not arbitrary hierarchy but ordered relation, by which the household, the church, and the civil order all stand. The supreme model is the Son’s own submission to the Father (1 Cor 15:28), and the Spirit’s ministering to the will of the Son—within an undivided God who is Himself a perfect order of love. Submission is never to be confused with the suppression of personhood, the silencing of conscience before God, or the toleration of sin in the one to whom one is subject; the apostles obey God rather than men when commanded to violate God’s law; the wife does not sin to please her husband; the saint does not bow to civil orders that command idolatry. But within God’s appointed orders and the limits of His Word, submission is the disposition of the Christian heart: a quiet, willing, glad placing of self under, in imitation of the Son and by the strength of the Spirit, for the good of the order, the honor of God, and the flourishing of all whom that order is meant to bless.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SUBMIT as to yield, resign, or surrender to the power, will, or authority of another; to refer; to leave or commit to the discretion or judgment of another.
webster_full: SUBMIT, v.t. — 1. To let down; to cause to sink or lower. 2. To yield, resign, or surrender to the power, will, or authority of another; to commit. Submit yourselves to your own husbands (Eph 5:22). 3. To refer; to leave or commit to the discretion or judgment of another; as, to submit a controversy to arbitrators.
SUBMIT, v.i. — To surrender; to yield one’s person to the power of another; to give up resistance; to be subject.
scriptures: James 4:7
Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.
Ephesians 5:21
Submitting yourselves one to another in the fear of God.
1 Peter 5:5
Likewise, ye younger, submit yourselves unto the elder. Yea, all of you be subject one to another, and be clothed with humility...
Hebrews 13:17
Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account.
corruption_summary: Submission is the most allergic word of the present age, conflated reflexively with abuse and oppression, so that the whole biblical network of ordered submissions—of all to God, of wife to husband, of child to parent, of citizen to magistrate, of saint to elder—is rejected in principle, with grave damage to household, church, and civil order alike.
corruption_paragraphs: The age has rendered submission almost unsayable. The word is conflated reflexively with abuse, oppression, suppression of personhood, and the silencing of the weak by the strong; and the whole network of ordered submissions Scripture commands—to God, to Christ, to civil authority, to elders, to husband, to parent—is rejected in principle as inherently demeaning. The result is the systematic disordering of the spheres that God’s appointed submissions are meant to hold together: marriages without a head and without a heart willing to lay itself down; churches in which no flock will be led and no elder is honored; civil society in which authority is presumed illegitimate and disobedience is the default register; and individual souls who have unlearned the very disposition of bowing under, even to God Himself. The pastoral cost is enormous; the cultural cost is greater.

Submission is also corrupted in the opposite direction by the abusive caricature in which submission is treated as servile, unconditional, and total—the wife is to submit to a husband who calls her to sin; the citizen is to obey magistrates ordering idolatry; the church member is to follow elders no matter what they preach. This is not biblical submission; it is the substitution of human tyranny for the ordered relations God commanded. The apostles set the rule: we ought to obey God rather than men. Within God’s orders and the limits of His Word, the saint submits gladly, in imitation of the Son who submitted to the Father; beyond those limits, the same saint stands and bears the consequences. Recover both ends: the principled refusal of every authority that commands sin, and the glad, willing, ordered submission to every authority that does not. The Christian is not a free agent; he is a placed agent—set, like the Son, in the order of His Father’s house.
roots_summary: Greek hupotassō (to arrange under, place in order under)—a military picture of troops in rank—and Hebrew kāna (to humble, be subdued): glad, ordered placing-of-self under God’s appointed authority.
roots_lines: Greek hupotassō (G5293) — to arrange under, subordinate, submit (military origin).
Greek hupotagē (G5292) — the noun: subjection, submission.
Hebrew kāna (H3665) — to humble, bring into subjection.
Hebrew shāphēl (H8213) — to be low, brought down—the humiliation that precedes ordered submission.
usage: Submission is the glad placing-of-self under in God’s appointed order—not the suppression of personhood and not the silencing of conscience.
The supreme model is the Son’s own submission to the Father; the saint’s submissions are imitations of His, in the strength of the same Spirit.
The age allergic to submission disorders every sphere God’s ordered submissions are meant to hold together—household, church, and civil order alike.
