etymology: From Latin testificari, “to bear witness,” from testis (witness) + facere (to make). Renders the Greek martureō, “to bear witness,” and diamarturomai, “to bear thorough witness, charge solemnly”; and the Hebrew ‘ūd, “to bear witness, testify.”
biblical_def: To testify is to bear witness—to declare under solemn responsibility what one has seen, heard, or received, with one’s name attached to the testimony and one’s person standing behind it. In Scripture, the verb is courtroom-shaped: a witness testifies to a fact, and the truth or falsity of his testimony is a matter of judgment, with severe penalties for false witness. The chief use of the word is christological and apostolic. The Father testifies to the Son: this is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. The Spirit testifies of Christ: he shall testify of me. The Scriptures testify of Christ: they are they which testify of me. The apostles are appointed as Christ’s witnesses: ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth. Their testimony is the founding deposit of Christian truth—the historical witness to the life, death, resurrection, and lordship of Jesus Christ, codified in the New Testament and proclaimed in the church’s mission. The ongoing testimony of the church is derivative of and bound to this apostolic deposit: every believer is to be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you, and the Spirit of God bears witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God. Testimony in the New Testament therefore has both an objective face (the apostolic witness to historical fact, summarized in the gospel) and a personal face (the believer’s own life and word standing behind the gospel he confesses). Both are essential; neither is the whole; and both together are what Christ means when He sends His church into the world as witnesses unto Him.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines TESTIFY as to make a solemn declaration, verbal or written, to establish some fact; to bear witness; to declare a fact or facts, especially in a court of justice; in scripture, to declare or publish solemnly.
webster_full: TESTIFY, v.i. — To make a solemn declaration, verbal or written, to establish some fact; to give testimony for the purpose of communicating to others a knowledge of something not known to them. In a court of justice, to make a solemn declaration under oath, for the purpose of establishing or making proof of some fact to a court.

TESTIFY, v.t. — 1. To bear witness to; to support the truth of by testimony. 2. To affirm or declare solemnly for the purpose of establishing a fact (1 Cor 15:15). 3. In scripture, to publish and declare freely (Acts 20:21).
scriptures: Acts 1:8

But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth.
John 15:26
But when the Comforter is come, whom I will send unto you from the Father, even the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father, he shall testify of me.
John 5:39
Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me.
1 Peter 3:15
...be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear.
corruption_summary: Testimony is corrupted by the self-referential turn of the age, which reduces it from witness-to-Christ to autobiography-about-me, and by the affective storytelling register that prizes emotional resonance over the propositional content of what is testified.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern evangelical ‘testimony’ has drifted from its New Testament moorings. In Scripture, to testify is to bear witness to Christ—to His person, His work, His resurrection, His lordship; the witness’s own story is the occasion, not the substance, of the testimony. In much contemporary use, the proportion has been inverted: the autobiography becomes the substance and Christ becomes the occasion, the testimony is judged by how moving the personal narrative is rather than by how clearly the gospel is set forth, and a generation rises that has heard many testimonies and very little explicit witness to who Christ is and what He has done. Recover the apostolic shape: testify to Him; tell your story only so far as it serves to make Him plain.

Testimony is also corrupted by the affective storytelling register that prizes emotional resonance over the propositional content of what is testified. The witness in the New Testament is courtroom-shaped: he says what is so. His testimony stands or falls by whether it is true. The believer’s answer to the man who asks a reason of the hope must include actual reasons—the historical fact of the resurrection, the propositions of the gospel, the doctrines that constitute the hope—and not only the texture of the believer’s experience. Recover both ends: the personal face (the believer’s life and word standing behind what he confesses) and the objective face (the apostolic content of the gospel itself, faithfully testified). The faithful witness is both: a real person bearing a real message about a real Christ.
roots_summary: Greek martureō (to bear witness) and diamarturomai (to bear thorough witness, charge solemnly); Hebrew ‘ūd (to bear witness)—the courtroom-shaped declaration of fact under solemn responsibility.
roots_lines: Greek martureō (G3140) — to bear witness, testify; the root behind martyr, the witness who seals his testimony with his blood.
Greek diamarturomai (G1263) — to bear thorough witness, charge solemnly—Paul’s frequent word for solemn testimony.
Greek marturia (G3141) — the noun: witness, testimony.
Hebrew ‘ūd (H5749) — to bear witness, testify, charge solemnly.
usage: Testifying is courtroom-shaped: the witness says what is so, with his name attached and his person standing behind it.
The apostolic testimony to Christ’s resurrection is the founding deposit of Christian truth—all subsequent witness is derivative of it and bound to it.
The modern testimony has often inverted the proportion: the autobiography becomes the substance and Christ becomes the occasion; the apostolic shape must be recovered.

etymology: From Old French trembler, from Latin tremulus (shaking), from tremere (to shake). Renders the Hebrew rā‘ad, “to tremble, quake,” chārēd, “to tremble with awe,” and the Greek tremō, “to tremble.”
biblical_def: To tremble in Scripture is the bodily expression of reverent fear before God—not the cringing terror of the slave before the tyrant, but the awed shaking of the creature standing in the presence of the holy Creator, the sinner standing before the throne of judgment, or the saint hearing the Word of his God with the weight that Word deserves. The pattern is set early: Israel at Sinai trembles before the voice of the LORD and the smoking mountain; Daniel in the presence of the heavenly messenger is left trembling and without strength; Isaiah in the throne-room cries woe is me, for I am undone; Habakkuk says when I heard, my belly trembled; my lips quivered at the voice; the disciples at the transfiguration were sore afraid. The LORD Himself names trembling as a mark of those He looks upon: to this man will I look, even to him that is poor and of a contrite spirit, and trembleth at my word. The New Testament continues the theme: the apostles charge the believer to work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, not because salvation is precarious but because it is awesome; James warns that even the devils believe and tremble—a fearful word against the doctrinaire who knows much and is unmoved. Trembling is no fashion of natural temperament; it is a Spirit-wrought response of the spiritually living soul to the holy God and His weighty Word. Its loss in any age is a sign that the doctrine of God has shrunk, that the holiness of God has been domesticated, and that the soul has lost the proper sense of His presence. Recover the doctrine of God in His holiness, and trembling returns of itself—the right and reverent shaking of the creature before the Creator and the sinner before the Savior in whose hand are the issues of life and death.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines TREMBLE as to shake involuntarily, as with fear, cold, or weakness; to quake; to shudder; to quiver; in scripture, to fear; to be affected with fear.
webster_full: TREMBLE, v.i. — 1. To shake involuntarily, as with fear, cold, or weakness; to quake; to shudder; to quiver. 2. To shake; to quiver, as the earth or the heavens. 3. In scripture, to fear; to be affected with fear; as, to tremble at the word of the LORD (Isa 66:2).
TREMBLING, n. — The act of shaking involuntarily; quaking; the state of being affected with fear or reverence.
scriptures: Philippians 2:12
Wherefore, my beloved, as ye have always obeyed... work out your own salvation with fear and trembling.
Isaiah 66:2
...but to this man will I look, even to him that is poor and of a contrite spirit, and trembleth at my word.
James 2:19
Thou believest that there is one God; thou doest well: the devils also believe, and tremble.
Acts 16:29
Then he called for a light, and sprang in, and came trembling, and fell down before Paul and Silas...
corruption_summary: Trembling is corrupted by the domesticated god of the present age—reduced to a friendly companion who issues no summons that shakes the soul—and by the casual register of worship and Scripture-reading that meets the holy God with no awe and no quaking at all.
corruption_paragraphs: The shrinking of the doctrine of God in the contemporary church has produced a generation that does not tremble. Where the saint of every preceding age met the holy God in the Word and at the Lord’s table with a reverence that shook the soul, the modern worshipper meets a domesticated god who issues no summons that quakes him: a god who is endlessly affirming, endlessly understanding, endlessly tolerant of whatever the worshipper brings; a god whose voice is the gentle whisper only and never the voice that shook Sinai. The result is worship without trembling, Scripture-reading without trembling, prayer without trembling, the Lord’s table approached without trembling—and a Christianity stripped of one of the marks Scripture itself names as the credential of the regenerate soul: him that trembleth at my word.

James’ rebuke is severe and quotable: thou believest that there is one God; thou doest well: the devils also believe, and tremble. The man who knows true doctrine and is unmoved by it is in worse case than the demon who at least trembles at what he knows. Recover the holiness of God, the weight of His Word, the reality of His presence, the seriousness of His judgments—and trembling returns of itself. The recovery is not artificial: the saint cannot be talked into trembling; he can only be set, by the Spirit, in the presence of the God who summons it. But the right setting—a high doctrine of God preached and sung, a Bible read as the actual voice of God, a Lord’s table approached as a meeting with the crucified and risen Christ—will produce the trembling that the contemporary register has so notably lost.
roots_summary: Hebrew rā‘ad (to tremble, quake), chārēd (to tremble with awe—Isa 66:2), and rāgaz (to be agitated, tremble); Greek tremō (to tremble)—the bodily expression of reverent fear before the holy God.
roots_lines: Hebrew rā‘ad (H7460) — to tremble, quake.
Hebrew chārēd (H2729) — to tremble with awe; cognate of the noun in Isa 66:2.
Hebrew rāgaz (H7264) — to be agitated, tremble, quake.
Greek tremō (G5141) — to tremble; used of the woman with the issue of blood, of the Philippian jailer, and of the demons (James 2:19).
usage: Trembling is the bodily expression of reverent fear before the holy God—the awed shaking of the creature, not the cringing of the slave.
To this man will I look, even to him that is poor and of a contrite spirit, and trembleth at my word—the LORD names trembling as a mark of those He regards.
The devils also believe, and tremble—the doctrinaire who knows and is unmoved is in worse case than the demon who at least trembles at what he knows.

etymology: From Old French waitier, “to watch, lie in wait, attend.” Renders the Hebrew qāvāh, “to bind together, wait expectantly,” yāchal, “to hope, wait,” and chākāh, “to wait, long for”; and the Greek apekdechomai, “to await eagerly,” and hupomenō, “to remain under, endure.”
biblical_def: To wait on the LORD is the great inward posture of the believing soul under the providence of God—a sustained, hope-filled, often painful expectancy that refuses to act in the flesh, to seize the matter into its own hand, or to abandon the promise as failed. The Hebrew qāvāh is striking: it pictures the binding together of strands into a cord, the soul drawn together in tension around the expected God. They that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint. Waiting is the discipline of saints in every age: David waiting for the kingdom while Saul hunted him; Joseph waiting in the prison; the patriarchs dying in faith without having received the promises; the church across the centuries waiting for the return of her Lord. It is a wait that is not idle: the waiting soul is praying, hoping, persevering, often laboring at present duties without seeing the larger outcome. The promise attached to it is large: strength renewed, salvation seen, the desired good obtained at the appointed hour—though often through delays the soul could not have imagined and would not have chosen. The deepest waiting is eschatological: the church waits for his Son from heaven; we look for that blessed hope, and the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ; the whole creation groans and travails in pain, waiting for the manifestation of the sons of God. Apart from waiting, faith degenerates into either fleshly self-action (Abraham’s Hagar) or despairing abandonment of the promise (Esau’s birthright for a bowl of stew). With waiting, faith ripens into the patience of the saints who, having seen the promises afar off, were persuaded of them, embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth—and obtained at last the city of God.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines WAIT as to stay or rest in expectation; to stop or remain stationary, till the arrival of some person or event; in scripture, to look for in expectation, with hope and trust.
webster_full: WAIT, v.i. — 1. To stay or rest in expectation; to stop or remain stationary, till the arrival of some person or event. 2. To stay in expectation; to rest in patience. 3. In scripture, to look for in expectation; to expect with hope and trust. I wait for the LORD; my soul doth wait, and in his word do I hope (Psa 130:5).
WAITING, ppr. — Staying in expectation; expecting with hope and trust.
scriptures: Isaiah 40:31
But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.
Psalm 27:14
Wait on the LORD: be of good courage, and he shall strengthen thine heart: wait, I say, on the LORD.
Lamentations 3:25-26
The LORD is good unto them that wait for him, to the soul that seeketh him. It is good that a man should both hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD.
Psalm 130:5-6
I wait for the LORD, my soul doth wait, and in his word do I hope. My soul waiteth for the Lord more than they that watch for the morning...
corruption_summary: Waiting is corrupted by the on-demand culture that has unlearned the discipline of patient hope—Amazon-day delivery has trained the soul to interpret any delay as failure, and the waiting saint is increasingly an alien temperament in a culture that cannot bear to wait for anything.
corruption_paragraphs: On-demand culture has unlearned the saint’s deepest discipline. Where the believing soul of every preceding age waited for harvests, for travel, for letters, for the long answer to long prayer, the contemporary soul has been trained by same-day delivery and instant streaming to interpret any delay as failure—and to bring the same impatience to God. Delayed answers are read as denied prayers; unfinished sanctification is read as ineffectual grace; the long pilgrimage of the Christian life is felt as a problem to be solved by acceleration rather than as the very means by which faith is matured. The Christian under God’s providence is increasingly an alien temperament in a culture that cannot bear to wait, and the discipline of waiting has been quietly displaced by the discipline of optimization and pursuit.

The biblical cure is not nostalgia but doctrine. Waiting is commanded because God’s purposes ripen in His seasons, not ours; because faith is proved and strengthened precisely in the long interval between promise and fulfillment; because the eschatological hope of the church is by definition a hope of what is not yet seen; and because the very act of waiting on the LORD is itself a renewing of strength, a mounting on eagle’s wings, a stillness in the soul that no amount of restless self-action can secure. Recover the doctrine and the saint recovers the temperament: a quiet, expectant, hope-filled waiting under God’s providence, refusing both the fleshly self-action that grasps the matter prematurely and the despair that abandons the promise as failed. The waiting church is the patient church; the patient church is the strong church; and the strong church will see the salvation of her God.
roots_summary: Hebrew qāvāh (to bind together, wait expectantly—Isa 40:31), yāchal (to hope, wait), chākāh (to wait, long for); Greek apekdechomai (to await eagerly) and hupomenō (to remain under, endure).
roots_lines: Hebrew qāvāh (H6960) — to wait, look eagerly for; the verb of Isa 40:31, pictured as the binding-together of strands.
Hebrew yāchal (H3176) — to wait, hope (in the LORD’s word).
Greek apekdechomai (G553) — to await eagerly, used of the church waiting for Christ’s return (Phil 3:20).
Greek hupomenō (G5278) — to remain under, endure, persevere—the active face of biblical waiting.
usage: Waiting on the LORD is not idleness but a sustained, hope-filled expectancy under His providence, refusing both fleshly self-action and despairing abandonment of the promise.
They that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength—the very act of waiting is itself a means of grace.
On-demand culture has trained the soul to read every delay as failure; the saint must be re-taught the patience of the church across the centuries.

etymology: From Old English wæccan, “to be awake, keep vigil,” cognate with wake. Renders the Greek grēgoreō, “to stay awake, be vigilant,” agrupneō, “to be sleepless,” and nēphō, “to be sober”; and the Hebrew shāqad, “to watch with intent,” and shāmar, “to keep, guard.”
biblical_def: To watch is the active spiritual vigilance commanded of every Christian during the long night before his Lord’s return—an alert, sober, prayerful, sentinel posture against the encroachments of the world, the flesh, the devil, and the unexpected hour of the Master’s coming. The figure is martial. Christ’s discourse on the Mount of Olives is its great charter: watch therefore: for ye know not what hour your Lord doth come... therefore be ye also ready: for in such an hour as ye think not the Son of man cometh. The same word is on His lips at Gethsemane: watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation; the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak. Peter, having slept on guard that night, writes years later with the lesson burned in: be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour. Paul charges the elders of Ephesus to watch, knowing that grievous wolves will enter the flock; he charges Timothy to watch in all things, endure afflictions, do the work of an evangelist; he charges all believers to watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong. The verb gathers up several distinct duties. There is the watch of personal vigilance against besetting sins and devil-set snares; the watch of corporate vigilance by elders over the flock against wolves and over their own teaching; the watch of prayerful sobriety, by which the soul is kept alert and not dulled by the spirit of the age; and the watch of eschatological readiness, by which the church lives as those who expect the Master at any hour. To lose any one of these watches is to be found asleep at the post the Lord set. To keep them is to be the wise virgin with her lamp trimmed, the faithful servant whom his Lord, when He cometh, shall find so doing.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines WATCH as to look with attention; to keep guard; to be vigilant; in scripture, to be in a state of constant attention to duty and to one’s spiritual interests; to keep awake.
webster_full: WATCH, v.i. — 1. To be awake; to be or continue without sleep. 2. To be attentive; to look with care; to keep guard; to be vigilant. 3. In scripture, to be in a state of constant attention to duty and to one’s spiritual interests; as, watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation (Matt 26:41).
WATCH, v.t. — To guard; to have in keeping; to tend; as, the shepherd watches his flock; the sentinel watches the camp.
scriptures: Matthew 24:42
Watch therefore: for ye know not what hour your Lord doth come.
Matthew 26:41
Watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation: the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.
1 Peter 5:8
Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour.
Watch ye therefore: for ye know not when the master of the house cometh... Lest coming suddenly he find you sleeping. And what I say unto you I say unto all, Watch.
corruption_summary: Watching is corrupted by the screen-consumption culture that has reassigned the very word to passive media consumption—to watch something now means to spectate, not to keep guard—and by the spiritual dulling of the age that has unlearned the sober, alert, sentinel posture the Bible commands.
corruption_paragraphs: The very word watch has been reassigned by the screen-consumption culture of the age. To watch now means to spectate—to consume a show, to look at a screen, to be entertained. The active, alert, sentinel sense of the verb has nearly disappeared from common usage, and with it the moral imagination required to hear Christ’s command to watch therefore as anything more than a metaphor. The believer of the present age is more often watching something than watching for something; the long hours of screen-time have trained the soul into a posture of passive consumption that is the opposite of biblical watchfulness; and the spiritual senses meant to be exercised by alert vigilance have been dulled by the constant flow of media designed to numb them.

Recover the doctrine, and recover the sentinel. The Christian is a soldier on watch in the night, with the enemy active and the Master returning at an unknown hour. He is to be sober, not under the influence of the spirit of the age; vigilant, not lulled by routine; prayerful, not relying on his own strength; ready, not surprised when the cry goes up that the Bridegroom comes. The elder watches over the flock, the parent over the household, the believer over his own heart, and the whole church over her Lord’s appointed hour. To keep these watches is the church’s ordinary discipline; to lose them is to be found asleep at the post when the King returns. The most damning verdict in Christ’s eschatological parables is the one He pronounces on the servant whom the Master cometh and finds sleeping. Recover watchfulness, and the church recovers her soldier’s gait.
roots_summary: Greek grēgoreō (to stay awake, be vigilant), nēphō (to be sober), and agrupneō (to be sleepless); Hebrew shāqad (to watch with intent) and shāmar (to keep, guard)—the sentinel posture of the church in the long night before her Lord’s return.
roots_lines: Greek grēgoreō (G1127) — to stay awake, be vigilant; the verb of Christ’s eschatological commands to watch.
Greek nēphō (G3525) — to be sober, vigilant; paired with watching in 1 Pet 5:8.
Greek agrupneō (G69) — to be sleepless, watchful; used of elders watching for souls (Heb 13:17).
Hebrew shāqad (H8245) — to watch with intent (the almond branch of Jer 1:11-12).
usage: Watching is the active sentinel posture of the church in the long night—sober, alert, prayerful, ready for the unknown hour of her Lord’s return.
Watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation—the discipline that Peter neglected at Gethsemane and learned to teach as be sober, be vigilant.
Screen-consumption culture has reassigned the very verb to passive spectating; the recovery of biblical watching is also the recovery of the soldier’s gait.

etymology: From Old English wræstlian, “to wrestle, struggle.” Renders the Hebrew ’ābaq, “to wrestle” (the rare verb used only of Jacob at Peniel), and the Greek noun palē, “wrestling” (used only of the Christian’s combat in Eph 6:12).
biblical_def: Wrestling, in Scripture, names two great combats: the night-long contending of Jacob with the Angel of the LORD at Peniel, and the spiritual warfare of the saint against principalities and powers, world-rulers of this darkness, and wicked spirits in heavenly places. Genesis 32: Jacob, alone at the brook Jabbok the night before he is to meet Esau, is met by a Man with whom he wrestles until the breaking of the day; the Man touches the hollow of his thigh and puts it out of joint; Jacob will not let Him go until He blesses him; the Man names him Israel, for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed; and Jacob calls the place Peniel, for I have seen God face to face, and my life is preserved. Out of that wrestling Jacob walks limping the rest of his days—and changed forever. The story is the great Old Testament parable of the soul’s holy contending with God in prayer: pressing the promise, refusing to let go, being broken in the wrestling, and emerging blessed, named, and lame. Ephesians 6 names the other wrestling: we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places. The Christian is in a real, unseen, hand-to-hand combat with invisible powers; the whole armor of God is given for it; and the means of standing in the evil day are the gospel of peace, the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, the sword of the Spirit, and prayer in the Spirit at all seasons. Wrestling therefore has both its inward face (the saint’s pleading and pressing with God in prayer) and its outward face (the church’s warfare against the unseen powers that contend for the souls of men). Both are arduous; neither is metaphor; and both are credentialed by the New Testament as part of the regular discipline of every saint.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines WRESTLE as to strive with arms extended, to throw the antagonist; to struggle; to strive, contend; in scripture, to contend in prayer or in spiritual conflict.
webster_full: WRESTLE, v.i. — 1. To strive with arms extended, as two men, who seize each other by the collar and arms, each endeavoring to throw the other. 2. To struggle; to strive; to contend; as, to wrestle with difficulties; to wrestle with temptations. 3. In scripture, to contend in prayer with great earnestness; to strive in spiritual conflict (Eph 6:12).
WRESTLING, n. — The act of striving to throw an antagonist; struggling; contention in prayer or spiritual conflict.
scriptures: Genesis 32:24-26

And Jacob was left alone; and there wrestled a man with him until the breaking of the day. And when he saw that he prevailed not against him, he touched the hollow of his thigh... And he said, Let me go, for the day breaketh. And he said, I will not let thee go, except thou bless me.
Ephesians 6:12
For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places.
Colossians 4:12
Epaphras... saluteth you, always labouring fervently for you in prayers, that ye may stand perfect and complete in all the will of God.
Romans 15:30
Now I beseech you, brethren, for the Lord Jesus Christ’s sake, and for the love of the Spirit, that ye strive together with me in your prayers to God for me.
corruption_summary: Wrestling is corrupted by the metaphorization of the age, which has reduced ‘wrestling with doubt’ or ‘wrestling with the text’ to a posture of intellectual sophistication that prides itself on never resolving anything—and by the parallel evaporation of the doctrine of real spiritual warfare against actual unseen powers.
corruption_paragraphs: The contemporary church has metaphorized wrestling beyond recognition. Wrestling with the text, wrestling with doubt, wrestling with my faith—the language is everywhere, but its content has hollowed. Where Jacob wrestled with God and was changed, where Epaphras labored fervently in prayer that the saints might stand complete, where Paul charged the Romans to strive together with me in your prayers, the modern wrestler often poses rather than contends: the wrestling becomes a posture of intellectual sophistication that prides itself on the wrestling and is suspicious of any actual resolution. The biblical pattern is the opposite. Jacob wrestled all night and would not let go until he was blessed; the wrestling was means, not end; the blessing was sought and obtained. Recover the pattern, and wrestling in prayer becomes again what it is in the Bible: a real holy contending with God for the promised blessing, by a soul that intends not to leave the wrestling without the answer.

Wrestling is also corrupted by the parallel evaporation of the doctrine of real spiritual warfare. Ephesians 6 is read as figurative encouragement rather than as the apostle’s plain assertion that the church is in a hand-to-hand combat with actual unseen powers, and that the armor of God is provided precisely because the combat is real. The result is a Christianity that takes neither face of biblical wrestling seriously: it does not contend with God in prayer for the blessing, and it does not contend with the powers of darkness in spiritual warfare for the souls of men and the standing of the church. Recover both. Be Jacob at Peniel; be Paul in his prayer-labors for the churches; be Epaphras laboring fervently. The blessing is given to wrestlers who do not let go.
roots_summary: Hebrew ’ābaq (to wrestle—only at Peniel) and Greek palē (wrestling—only in Eph 6:12): the saint’s holy contending with God in prayer and the church’s real warfare against unseen powers.
roots_lines: Hebrew ’ābaq (H79) — to wrestle; the rare verb used only of Jacob’s wrestling at Peniel.
Greek palē (G3823) — wrestling, struggle, combat; used only in Eph 6:12 of spiritual warfare.
Greek agōnizōmai (G75) — to contend, strive, agonize; used of Epaphras’s prayer-wrestling in Col 4:12.
Greek sunagōnizōmai (G4865) — to strive together with—Paul’s appeal in Rom 15:30.
usage: Wrestling has two great faces in Scripture: the saint’s holy contending with God in prayer, and the church’s combat against unseen principalities and powers.
Jacob walked limping the rest of his days—the wrestling broke him and blessed him both, as it always does.
Metaphorized ‘wrestling with doubt’ that never resolves is not biblical wrestling; Jacob would not let go until he was blessed.

etymology: From Old English gieldan, “to pay, render, give back.” Renders the Greek paristēmi, “to present, place beside, yield” (the technical Romans 6 verb), and the Hebrew nāthan, “to give,” and ‘āsah, “to make, produce.”
biblical_def: To yield, in the central New Testament sense, is to present—deliberately, willingly, irrevocably—the members of one’s body to a master, for use as instruments. Paul’s great Romans 6 charter is unmistakable: neither yield ye your members as instruments of unrighteousness unto sin: but yield yourselves unto God, as those that are alive from the dead, and your members as instruments of righteousness unto God. The picture is of a regenerate man, raised with Christ, choosing day by day to whom he will present his body, his tongue, his eyes, his hands, his thought-life, his time, his money, his sexuality, his strength: to sin as a deposed master, or to God as the new and rightful Lord. Yielding in this sense is not passive surrender but active presentation; it is not a one-time crisis decision but the daily disposition of the believer in real moral choices; and it is the precise hinge on which practical sanctification turns. The man who yields his members to sin will be the servant of sin to whom he yields; the man who yields his members to God will, in the very act, be acting out the new identity that grace has already conferred. Yielding has a second sense in Scripture: the bearing of fruit (the ground yields her increase; the field yields a harvest; the saint, abiding in the Vine, yields fruit unto God). The two senses converge: the man who yields his members to God yields, by that very yielding, the fruit of righteousness in his life. A third sense in James 3 commends the wisdom from above as willing to yield—eupeithēs, easy to be entreated, open, persuadable, not stiff-necked in self-will. All three senses are biblical, and all three describe the Christian: a man who has presented his members to God, who bears the fruit of righteousness in his life, and whose temper is open and reasonable, not rigid and contentious.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines YIELD as to give in return for labor expended; to produce, as fruit, profit, issues; to give up, to resign, to surrender; in scripture, to present or surrender to God.
webster_full: YIELD, v.t. — 1. To produce, as fruit, profit, or issues; as, the earth yields her increase; the field yields a harvest. 2. To give in return for labor expended; to produce as a reward or recompence. 3. To give up, as claim or possession; to resign; to surrender; to relinquish. 4. To allow; to grant; to admit; as, to yield a point; to yield priority.
YIELD, v.i. — 1. To give up the contest; to submit. 2. To comply with; as, to yield to entreaty. 3. In scripture, to present or surrender oneself or one’s members to God (Rom 6:13).
scriptures: Romans 6:13

Neither yield ye your members as instruments of unrighteousness unto sin: but yield yourselves unto God, as those that are alive from the dead, and your members as instruments of righteousness unto God.
Romans 6:19
...for as ye have yielded your members servants to uncleanness and to iniquity unto iniquity; even so now yield your members servants to righteousness unto holiness.
James 3:17
But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, and easy to be intreated, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy.
John 15:5
I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing.
corruption_summary: Yielding is corrupted, on one side, by the passive-surrender misreading that empties the active presentation Paul commands; and on the other, by the cultural register that treats yielding as weakness—the rigid self-will that mistakes inflexibility for conviction and cannot bend even where the wisdom from above is plainly easy to be entreated.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 6’s yielding is sometimes preached as if it were a single mystical surrender, a let-go-and-let-God passivity by which the believer turns the wheel over to God and ceases to act. The text says the opposite. Paul commands an active, deliberate presentation of the members of the body, day by day, in the real moral choices that fill a Christian life: yield your members servants to righteousness unto holiness. The yielding is not passivity; it is precisely the act of presenting. The sanctified man is not the man who has stopped acting and waits for God to act through him; he is the man who, having been raised with Christ, deliberately presents his body, his tongue, his eyes, his time, his money, his sexuality, to God for use as instruments of righteousness—and who refuses to present them as instruments of unrighteousness. Recover the Romans 6 grammar and the doctrine returns to its New Testament force.

Yielding is also corrupted by the cultural register that treats it as weakness. The hard, contentious, stiff-necked temper that mistakes inflexibility for conviction is at home in much of the contemporary church, and the wisdom from above’s commendation of being easy to be entreated—a posture of being open, persuadable, willing to yield where Scripture and good cause counsel it—sounds to such ears like compromise. It is not. The biblical Christian yields his members to God in active presentation; he yields the fruit of righteousness in his life by abiding in the Vine; and he yields, in personal dealings, with the open and reasonable spirit James commends. The man who cannot yield in any of these three senses has not yet learned what the Spirit of God produces in His people—and is in no position to lead, teach, or contend for anything, because he cannot bend without breaking.
roots_summary: Greek paristēmi (to present, place beside—the technical Rom 6 verb of yielding the body’s members to a master); Hebrew nāthan (to give) and ‘āsah (to produce, bear fruit); Greek eupeithēs (easy to be entreated, willing to yield—James 3:17).
roots_lines: Greek paristēmi (G3936) — to present, place beside, yield; the verb of Rom 6:13 and 12:1 (present your bodies a living sacrifice).
Greek eupeithēs (G2138) — easy to be entreated, willing to yield (James 3:17).
Hebrew nāthan (H5414) — to give; the base verb of giving and yielding in the OT.
Hebrew ‘āsah (H6213) — to do, make, produce; used of trees and ground yielding fruit (Gen 1:11-12).
usage: Yielding the members in Romans 6 is active presentation, not passive surrender—the daily choice of which master will use one’s body, tongue, eyes, and time.
The branch in the Vine yields fruit; the wisdom from above yields to good cause; the saint yields his members to God—three biblical yieldings, one Christian.
Stiff-necked inflexibility that mistakes itself for conviction has unlearned the easy-to-be-entreated temper of the heavenly wisdom; biblical yielding is strength, not weakness.

etymology: From Latin adjurare, “to swear to, charge under oath,” from ad- (to) + jurare (to swear). Renders the Hebrew shāba in the hiphil, “to cause to swear, charge under oath,” and the Greek horkizō and exorkizō, “to put under oath.”
biblical_def: To adjure is to charge another with the most solemn weight—to lay upon him an oath, or its equivalent, by which the matter charged is bound to God Himself, and the one charged is obligated under the most awful sanction Scripture knows. Adjuration is therefore a peculiar speech-act: not ordinary command, not mere request, but a solemn binding under oath that calls God to witness and Himself to vindicate or punish the response. The Old Testament sets the pattern: Joshua adjures the people not to rebuild Jericho upon pain of curse; Saul adjures the army not to eat until evening; the high priest in the Christ-trial adjures Jesus by the living God to say whether He be the Christ. The New Testament continues the pattern in several gravities: the demon adjures Jesus by God not to torment him; Paul charges the Thessalonians by the Lord that his epistle be read to all the holy brethren; the apostle adjures Timothy before God and the Lord Jesus Christ to keep the charge entrusted to him without partiality. Adjuration is to be reserved for matters of the highest seriousness and to be used with the gravity proper to invoking God’s own oath. Christ’s own discourse warns against the trivializing of oaths in everyday speech—swear not at all... but let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay—and the early church was schooled against the casual, profane swearing of the surrounding pagan culture; but Christ Himself answered under adjuration in the trial before Caiaphas, and the apostles repeatedly bound their charges under solemn invocation of God. Adjuration therefore stands as the proper, weighty extreme of biblical speech: not common, not casual, but kept for the moments when the matter at hand calls for the most solemn possible binding of the conscience under God’s own witness.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ADJURE as to charge, bind, or command on oath, or under the penalty of a curse; to charge earnestly and solemnly.
webster_full: ADJURE, v.t. — 1. To charge, bind, or command on oath, or under the penalty of a curse. Joshua adjured them at that time, saying, Cursed be the man before the Lord, that riseth up and buildeth this city Jericho (Josh 6:26). 2. To charge earnestly and solemnly. I adjure thee by the living God (Matt 26:63).
ADJURATION, n. — The act of adjuring; a solemn charging on oath, or under the penalty of a curse; the form of oath.
scriptures: Joshua 6:26
And Joshua adjured them at that time, saying, Cursed be the man before the LORD, that riseth up and buildeth this city Jericho.
Matthew 26:63
But Jesus held his peace. And the high priest answered and said unto him, I adjure thee by the living God, that thou tell us whether thou be the Christ, the Son of God.
1 Thessalonians 5:27
I charge you by the Lord that this epistle be read unto all the holy brethren.
1 Timothy 5:21
I charge thee before God, and the Lord Jesus Christ, and the elect angels, that thou observe these things without preferring one before another, doing nothing by partiality.
corruption_summary: Adjuration is corrupted, on one side, by the wholesale unfamiliarity of the present age, which no longer recognizes the solemn category of speech at all, and on the other by the trivializing profanity that drops God’s name into ordinary speech as filler—both the substantive doctrine and the soberness about the third commandment having been lost together.
corruption_paragraphs: Adjuration as a category of speech has largely disappeared from the modern Christian’s vocabulary. The believer of an earlier era could distinguish ordinary speech, formal request, solemn charge, and adjuration under oath, and could mark the third commandment’s gravity by reserving God’s name to its proper weight; the modern believer often cannot. The result is a flattening of all speech registers into one, the loss of the solemn moments in which God’s witness is properly invoked, and the inability to recognize what is happening when the high priest adjures Christ or when Paul charges Timothy before God and the elect angels. Recover the category, and the believer recovers also a richer sense of the proper weight of his own speech and the proper restraint that ought to govern invocation of God’s name.

The opposite corruption is the trivializing profanity that drops God’s name and the name of Christ into ordinary speech as exclamation, filler, or expletive—and that has so saturated the contemporary verbal environment that even believers absorb it almost unconsciously. The third commandment is severe: thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain; for the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain. Where adjuration has been forgotten and profanity has been normalized, the church’s witness to the holiness of God’s name is weakened at its root. Recover both ends: keep God’s name from the trivial uses of casual speech, and reserve adjuration for the solemn moments where the gravity of the matter genuinely warrants it. The result is a believer whose ordinary yea is yea and whose nay is nay, and whose solemn charges, when they come, carry the weight of the One whose witness they invoke.
roots_summary: Hebrew shāba (hiphil—to cause to swear, charge under oath) and Greek horkizō, exorkizō (to put under oath)—the most solemn category of biblical speech, binding the conscience under God’s own witness.
roots_lines: Hebrew shāba (H7650, hiphil) — to cause to swear, to adjure, to charge under oath.
Greek horkizō (G3726) — to put under oath, adjure (Mark 5:7, the demon to Christ).
Greek exorkizō (G1844) — to charge under oath solemnly (Matt 26:63, the high priest to Christ).
Greek enorkizō (G1722-3726) — to put under solemn charge (1 Thess 5:27, Paul to the church).
usage: Adjuration is the most solemn category of biblical speech—the charging of another under oath, with God Himself called to witness.
Christ answered under adjuration before Caiaphas; Paul adjured Timothy before God and the elect angels—the category is biblical and weighty.
Where adjuration is forgotten and profanity is normalized, both the substantive doctrine and the third commandment’s gravity are lost together.

etymology: From Latin circumcidere, “to cut around,” from circum (around) + caedere (to cut). Renders the Hebrew mūl, “to circumcise,” and the Greek peritemnō, “to cut around.”
biblical_def: To circumcise is to apply the covenant sign given to Abraham and his seed—the cutting away of the foreskin of every male child of the household at the eighth day, the bloody token in the body of the everlasting covenant God made with Abraham and his seed after him. This is my covenant, which ye shall keep, between me and you and thy seed after thee; Every man child among you shall be circumcised... and it shall be a token of the covenant betwixt me and you. Circumcision is therefore not first a hygienic, ethnic, or cultural practice but a covenantal sign of belonging—the seal of the righteousness of the faith that Abraham had yet being uncircumcised, the mark of the people God claimed as His own, the bloody anticipation of a deeper cutting away that the prophets and apostles will identify as the circumcision of the heart. Moses commands it: circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no more stiffnecked; Jeremiah pleads it: circumcise yourselves to the LORD, and take away the foreskins of your heart; Paul completes it: he is a Jew, which is one inwardly; and circumcision is that of the heart, in the spirit, and not in the letter; and again, in whom also ye are circumcised with the circumcision made without hands, in putting off the body of the sins of the flesh by the circumcision of Christ. Under the New Covenant, physical circumcision has been fulfilled and superseded—the apostles fought a decisive battle at Jerusalem against the Judaizers who would have laid it upon Gentile believers as required for salvation; baptism has succeeded it as the covenant sign for the people of God; and what circumcision pointed to—the heart cut, the flesh put off, the soul covenantally claimed—is now wrought spiritually in every regenerate believer by the Spirit of God on the ground of the work of Christ. To miss this trajectory is to misread the whole flow of redemptive history; to follow it is to see, in the ancient bloody sign of Abraham’s seed, the gospel of the heart-circumcised people of God in Christ.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines CIRCUMCISE as to cut off the prepuce or foreskin, according to the Jewish law; in a spiritual sense, to purify the heart from sinful affections.
webster_full: CIRCUMCISE, v.t. — 1. To cut off the prepuce or foreskin of males, according to the Jewish law; a religious rite or ceremony, the token of the covenant between God and Abraham and his posterity (Gen 17). 2. In a spiritual sense, to purify the heart from sinful affections (Deut 10:16; Rom 2:29).

CIRCUMCISION, n. — The act of cutting off the prepuce or foreskin; a Jewish rite, the token of the covenant with Abraham. Spiritually, the putting away of the sins of the flesh by the regenerating work of the Spirit.
scriptures: Genesis 17:10-11

This is my covenant, which ye shall keep, between me and you and thy seed after thee; Every man child among you shall be circumcised. And ye shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin; and it shall be a token of the covenant betwixt me and you.
Deuteronomy 10:16
Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no more stiffnecked.
Romans 2:29
But he is a Jew, which is one inwardly; and circumcision is that of the heart, in the spirit, and not in the letter; whose praise is not of men, but of God.
Colossians 2:11
In whom also ye are circumcised with the circumcision made without hands, in putting off the body of the sins of the flesh by the circumcision of Christ.
corruption_summary: Circumcision is corrupted, on one side, by the reduction of the discussion to a purely medical-cosmetic debate that flattens the covenantal-theological dimension; and on the other, by the Judaizing error of every age that would re-impose the Old Covenant sign upon the New Covenant people of God, missing the redemptive-historical trajectory from sign to fulfillment.
corruption_paragraphs: The contemporary discussion of circumcision is almost wholly medical-cosmetic—debates over neonatal pain, parental consent, hygiene benefits, and cultural appropriation—with the covenantal-theological dimension that occupies the biblical text dropped almost entirely from view. The Christian who reads Scripture closely will not flatten the topic to such terms. Circumcision in the Bible is first and centrally a covenant sign—the bloody token of God’s claim on Abraham and his seed, the seal of the righteousness of faith, the anticipation of the deeper heart-circumcision wrought by the Spirit on the ground of Christ’s work. To read the biblical material as if it were principally about pediatric medicine is to miss the theological architecture of the Old Testament and the apostolic argument of Romans 2–4, Galatians, and Colossians 2.

The opposite corruption is the Judaizing error that would re-impose the Old Covenant sign upon the New Covenant people of God—the precise error the apostles confronted at the Jerusalem council in Acts 15 and which Paul fought to the death of his ministry in Galatians. Under the New Covenant, physical circumcision has been fulfilled and superseded by the spiritual circumcision of the heart wrought by the Spirit on the ground of Christ’s work and signified outwardly in baptism; to insist upon physical circumcision as required for salvation or covenant standing is to fall from grace and to declare that Christ has profited the believer nothing. Read the redemptive-historical arc properly: the sign was given to Abraham, kept by Israel under the Law, anticipated the heart-circumcision the prophets pleaded for, and is fulfilled at the cross—where the body of the sins of the flesh is put off by the circumcision of Christ for all who are united to Him by faith.
roots_summary: Hebrew mūl (to circumcise) and Greek peritemnō (to cut around): a covenant sign in the flesh that anticipates the deeper circumcision of the heart, wrought by the Spirit on the ground of the cross.
roots_lines: Hebrew mūl (H4135) — to circumcise; both physical (Gen 17) and metaphorical (Deut 10:16, heart).
Greek peritemnō (G4059) — to cut around, circumcise; literal and figurative.
Greek peritomē (G4061) — circumcision (the noun); also of the spiritual circumcision in Col 2:11.
Greek akrobustia (G203) — uncircumcision, the foreskin; the contrast term in Romans 2–4.
usage: Circumcision is first a covenant sign—the bloody token of God’s claim on Abraham’s seed, anticipating the heart-circumcision the prophets pleaded for.
Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no more stiffnecked—Moses already names the deeper reality the sign pointed to.

Under the New Covenant, physical circumcision is fulfilled and superseded by baptism and by the circumcision made without hands; to re-impose it upon Gentile believers is the Judaizing error Paul confronted to the end.
